newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU clash over Italy to make EMU deal tougher.
newsitem.headline: EU clash over Italy to make EMU deal tougher.

text.p: The furore unleashed in Rome on Wednesday by reports that European Union monetary officials were considering delaying Italy's entry into Europe's single currency could make a compromise solution much harder to achieve.

Analysts said the sharp and unequivocal chorus of denials over a Financial Times article that suggested a face-saving deal was in the works underscored the difficulty the 15-nation bloc would have in finding common ground.

Moreover, the vehemence with which the Italian government denied the charges will ultimately make it even more determined to meet the 1999 criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), causing difficulties with its partners.
"I can't see that it makes things easier and at the margin it might make life more difficult," said Martin Brookes, international economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
"If people are publicly talking about delay, Italy has to become more entrenched," he added.

Responding to the news accounts, Prime Minister Romano Prodi said: "The Italian government...deplores the constant repetition of false stories and unjustified statements, including from authoritative media, which have no foundation whatsoever."

One concern highlighted by Wednesday's debate was the prospect that the Italian government might relax its efforts at meeting the economic requirements for EMU if it is excluded from the first wave of entrants.
Several analysts said financial markets had remained relatively calm over the idea of Rome entering EMU after 1999.
"The markets' view is a reasonably mature one," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.
"It doesn't matter much as long as they're in a year or two later," he added.
But should a delayed entry result in domestic and political turbulence in Italy, European bond and currency markets could quickly reverse their benign attitude.
From an impartial standpoint, several said Italy had little justification in demanding that it be a founding member of EMU.

Within the so-called "Club Med" countries, its track record on inflation and public deficits was less stellar than Spain and Portugal. The end result of such differences would be how EU leaders could finesse allowing Spain and Portugal into the single currency on time and not Italy.
"I think France and Germany are working away to split this group up," added Marshall.

Perhaps most ironic is the fact that Italy's steadfast position would make strict application of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria even more likely, putting countries like Germany and France in an uncomfortable light. Both of the so-called EU core nations have problems with their own budget deficits against a backdrop of sluggish growth and rising unemployment.
The logic behind this view revolves around the fact that should Italy be excluded because it could not meet the criteria in a strict sense, there would be little leeway for others.
"The Italian problem is pushing the EU into a very strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty," said Brookes of Goldman Sachs.
Should France and Germany fail to meet their own demands, it would be very awkward indeed for them to then exclude others who were marginally worse.
